tools.name: mcp__pixellab__create_character
tools.description:
Queue character creation. Returns immediately with character ID. Use get_character to check status. It takes NO seed and cannot be made reproducible — unusually for the family, since create_character_pro_flash and create_character_state both do; to keep a look across characters pass style_character_id or a reference image instead.

Cost: the mode decides it, and standard is the cheap one — 1 generation at ANY size, 4 or 8 directions. mode='v3' from scratch draws the sprite AND its 8 rotations, by longest side: 2 for 16-90; 3 for 91-128; 4 for 129-156; 5 for 157-181; 6 for 182-202; 7 for 203-221; 8 for 222-239; 9 for 240-256. Passing a reference sprite drops the drawing step and prices the reference's OWN width times height — ceil(w*h*8/65536), minimum 1 — NOT the square ladder above, so a tall sprite is cheap: 64x64, 48x80 and 64x96 are all 1, 128x128 is 2, and 32x256 is 1 where drawing it from text would be 9. Setting size makes the output square, and then the square rule applies. Supplying every direction yourself is an import, 0.25 generations. mode='pro' prices a 3x3 grid and is the dear one: 10 up to 85px, 15 for 86-113, 25 for 114-128, which is also its size cap (v3 is the only mode that reaches 256px).

Which mode: v3 (default) for heroes, enemies and NPCs: clearly more detailed sprites than standard, 2 generations up to 88 px. For a quadruped from text, create_character_pro_flash(template_id=...) at 64 px. Pro when a new character must match an existing one (style_character_id) or to follow concept art. Standard for the lowest cost.
Standard mode: 1 generation, 4 or 8 directions, ~2-5 min. Style params are soft guidance (the model tries to follow them but results may vary).
Pro mode: 10-25 generations, always 8 directions, higher quality. Ignores all style/proportions params. Accepts style_character_id to match an existing 8-direction character's style, and concept_image_url to design the character from concept art, a painting or a photo.
Pro mode only: pass `palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) for a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any Lospec palette): all 8 directions are drawn for it and every pixel is one of its colours. `max_colors` is Pro-only too.
v3 mode: 2-9 generations, 8 directions, highest quality. Outline and detail are soft guidance; shading/proportions ignored.
v3 + reference_image_base64 / reference_image_url: rotates YOUR south-facing sprite into 8 (or 4) directions — use this (not create_8_direction_object) to turn an existing character sprite into a full character. Works for humanoids and quadrupeds (pass body_type="quadruped" + template). Add direction_images for directions you already drew; v3 fills only the rest.
v3 without a reference image draws the sprite itself and is humanoid only.
Humanoid: bipedal characters with proportion customization.
Quadruped: 4-legged animals — requires template param (bear, cat, dog, horse, lion).

PixelLab AI-powered pixel art generation service.

Use of this service is subject to PixelLab's Terms of Service:
https://pixellab.ai/termsofservice

This MCP server provides programmatic access to generate:
- Characters with multiple directional views
- Character animations
- Isometric tiles
- Top-down tilesets for game maps
- Sidescroller tilesets for platformer games

All generation operations are non-blocking and return job IDs for status tracking.
Requires PixelLab subscription (with credit fallback support).

**Pixel tools (free, exact, you are the artist)**: one command line, pixelart_workbench(argv=[...]), inspects, edits, draws and animates pixel art by your own decisions; combine it with the AI tools above. Start with pixelart_workbench(argv=['describe', 'start'], mode='low'|'high') — low acts directly with few tokens, high plans out loud and reviews every frame. Animated effects (spells, hits, explosions, auras): vfx_workbench(argv=['describe', 'start']) — same ids, exports to the user's My effects.

**Git access**: Clone and push game project source code with standard git.
Use `list_projects` to see your projects and their git clone URLs.

exec tool declaration:
```ts
declare const tools: { mcp__pixellab__create_character(args: { body_type?: "humanoid" | "quadruped"; concept_image_base64?: string | null; concept_image_url?: string | null; description: string; detail?: "low detail" | "medium detail" | "high detail"; direction_images?: { east?: string | null; north?: string | null; "north-east"?: string | null; "north-west"?: string | null; "south-east"?: string | null; "south-west"?: string | null; west?: string | null; } | null; max_colors?: number | null; mode?: "standard" | "pro" | "v3"; n_directions?: 4 | 8; name?: string | null; outline?: "single color black outline" | "single color outline" | "selective outline" | "lineless"; palette?: Array<string> | null; palette_name?: string | null; proportions?: string | null; reference_image_base64?: string | null; reference_image_url?: string | null; shading?: "flat shading" | "basic shading" | "medium shading" | "detailed shading"; size?: number | null; style_character_id?: string | null; template?: string | null; text_guidance_scale?: number; view?: "low top-down" | "high top-down" | "side" | "oblique"; }): Promise<CallToolResult>; };
```

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_upload_url
tools.description:
Get a URL to upload a local image file to, without needing your API token.

Use it whenever you have an image on disk and a tool wants an image: send
the file with one curl, and pass the `upload:<id>` it returns to any
parameter that takes an image URL (image_urls, reference_image_url,
init_image_url, a style_image "url" ...). This avoids pasting base64 into a
tool call, which clients truncate and can corrupt. Free.

The URL works for 15 minutes and for any number of files. Uploads are kept
3 days. An animated GIF keeps all its frames.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_character
tools.description:
Get character details, rotation URLs, animations, and download link.
Branches by status: processing (progress+ETA), failed (error+retry), completed (full data).

Download: three ways out, and the last one needs no HTTP at all.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/download` is a ZIP of every completed state in the
group — `?states=` narrows it, taking the state IDS this tool prints on
its `state:` lines, not their names — laid out as
`<state>/rotations/<direction>.png` and
`<state>/animations/<name>/<direction>/frame_000.png` (frame_NNN, 3 digits,
from 000), plus `<state>/portrait.png` and `<state>/vocal/grid.png` where
those exist, and a top-level `metadata.json` giving each state's size,
directions, view, template_id and a `frames` map listing every file — so
the per-direction frame counts are in there as the list lengths. A frame
storage lost shows up as `MISSING_FRAMES.txt` rather than a short ZIP.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one sheet PNG + its layout
JSON for THIS state only: row 0 is the rotations, then one row per
animation-direction, uniform cells sized to the largest frame with the rest
transparent padding (nothing is ever resized), and the JSON gives
`cell_size`, `sheet_size`, `columns`, `pivot: "cell-center"` and a row list
naming each row's animation, `animation_group_id`, direction and
frame_count.
To get the pixels back INLINE, with no download and nothing charged:
`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns that animation's frames as one sheet image in the tool result, with
the canvas and frame durations — `<animation>` is the display name, type or
[group: ...] id this tool prints. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (sheets hold at most 1024 px a side).
